eligibility_reason: TAME is a training-free MLLM personalized assistant whose contribution is a 'double-memory' mechanism: a Dynamic State (DS) Memory and a Static Personalized (SP) Memory that the model itself writes at run time from each dialogue turn and later reads to condition its own future responses (p. 2, 'we first introduce a fresh Dynamic State Memory ... to continually track multimodal contextual information'; 'we propose a new Static Personalized Memory'). Algorithm 1 (p. 7) shows the full write/retrieve/update loop across turns: memory construction from historical dialogue (lines 1-13), retrieval for the current query via Retrieve-then-Align Augmented Generation (lines 14-24), and memory update with the new interaction (lines 25-28) -- state written at run time and reused across turns, satisfying I1. Year 2025 (I2, arXiv Dec 2025 per p. 1 header); English (I3); text retrievable (I4). Not hardware/cache work, not parametric-only, not a fixed never-written corpus (the whole point of DS/SP Memory is that the assistant writes to them every turn, ruling out E1-E3); this is primary research proposing a new benchmark and baseline, not a survey (rules out E4); memory is the paper's central, title-level contribution, not incidental (rules out E5); it is a full paper with algorithm, benchmark, ablations and appendix, well over four pages (rules out E7). The paper calls the system a 'personalized MLLM assistant' rather than using the word 'agent' anywhere in the given pages, but it meets the functional test in I1 (writes and retrieves cross-turn state to condition future behaviour) and additionally orchestrates external tools (an open-set grounding/segmentation model, embedding models) as part of its pipeline (p. 7, Section 4.5), so E6 is judged not to apply.

facets.justification: The paper's named contribution is the combination of two differentiated stores and the mechanism that moves content between them: 'TAME endows MLLMs with double memories to manage the temporal and persistent variations of each personalized concept in a differentiated manner ... we introduce a novel Double Memory Transition mechanism, which updates the long-term attributes in the SP Memory by referencing the DS Memory, while discarding outdated short-term attributes' (p. 2). This is not an incidental second store; the ablation in Table 3 (p. 9) specifically isolates 'w/o DS Memory' vs 'w/o SP Memory' vs 'w/o Memory', confirming the tiering between the two stores is what is being evaluated.

The headline mechanism is explicitly a store-editing transition, not a pure append: DS Memory entries are added, kept, updated into SP Memory, or removed as outdated (p. 2, 'discarding outdated short-term attributes'; Algorithm 1 p. 7, lines 6-11, 'if trigger ... Update SP Memory by referencing DS Memory' and 'Remove outdated short-term attributes if |Md| > threshold'). The worked example on p. 28 shows the same operations by name against a running memory: 'Add DS Memory 1', 'Update DS Memory 1 to SP Memory 1', 'Remove DS Memory 1', 'Keep DS Memory 1' -- existing entries are updated, merged into the persistent store, and deleted as new dialogue arrives.

Section 4.5 / eq. 9-10 (p. 7) and Algorithm 1 lines 15-22 describe a declared two-stage combination: an entity image is matched to a concept id by embedding similarity across visual and textual features (eq. 10, a similarity ranking step), the matched memories are then filtered by exact concept-id equality ('Locate memory Mdc <- {(Cid, Attr) in Md | Cid = c}', a structured/exact-match query), and finally 'the most relevant E items with respect to the user query' are pulled from that filtered set before an explicit alignment step (Retrieve-then-Align Augmented Generation, RA2G) fuses the retrieved multi-memory content with the query. The paper names this staged retrieve-then-align combination as its own paradigm, which is the declared fusion rule the hybrid value requires.

TAME is assessed only on LCMP, a benchmark the authors themselves constructed (p. 1 abstract, p. 9 Table 3 ablation with metrics ACC-C, ACC-F, SPR-L, SPR-S), with no mention in the given pages of real users, a fielded deployment, or any setting outside the authors' own experiment. This is a controlled, in-lab technique evaluation, coded conservatively as validation rather than evaluation per the guide's precedence rule.

Table 3 (p. 9) reports TAME and ablated variants (w/o DS Memory, w/o SP Memory, w/o Memory, w/o Alignment, w/o Retrieval) scored on four LCMP metrics against a fixed benchmark; the conclusion (p. 9) reiterates evaluation 'on LCMP' as the evidence base.

The paper repeatedly names TAME itself as an architecture: 'we introduce a novel training-free and state-aware framework TAME' (p. 1 abstract) and 'We introduce TAME, a novel training-free and state-aware personalized MLLM assistant powered by double memories' (p. 2 contributions list) -- an organising architecture (double memory + RA2G) rather than a single algorithmic technique, dataset, tool release, model, or metric.
